title: Deformation of sine-Gordon two-soliton solutions in $\varphi^4$ kink-antikink configurations
authors: Aliakbar Moradi Marjaneh, Danial Saadatmand, Fabiano C. Simas, Jarah Evslin, Dionisio Bazeia
abstract: In this work, we construct analytical kink-antikink $(K\bar{K})$ configurations in the non-integrable $\varphi^4$ model by mapping exact solutions of the integrable sine-Gordon system via a field deformation. This procedure yields two distinct classes of configurations, parametrized by the initial half-separation and velocity. We compare these profiles with the standard additive superposition Ansatz in terms of vacuum structure and equation-of-motion residuals, deriving explicit closed-form expressions for the corresponding integrated squared residuals. For small separations, the mapped soliton-antisoliton configurations exhibit appreciably smaller residuals than the naive superposition Ansatz, which in turn performs better than the mapped two-soliton configurations. Although the mapped fields are not exact solutions of the $\varphi^4$ equation of motion, they provide mathematically consistent, topologically sound, and physically motivated initial data for numerical studies of kink-antikink scattering and resonance phenomena.
summary: This work develops an analytical method to approximate kink-antikink configurations in the non-integrable $\varphi^4$ model by deforming known solutions from the integrable sine-Gordon system. By quantifying the error using integrated residuals, the authors demonstrate that their deformed solutions significantly outperform the standard linear superposition method, offering superior initial data for numerical simulations of soliton scattering.

main_result: The deformation method yields two classes of K$ ar{	ext{K}}$ configurations whose integrated squared residuals are significantly smaller than the naive additive superposition Ansatz, providing better initial data for numerical studies.
method: The core method involves a field deformation mapping from the integrable sG system to the non-integrable $\varphi^4$ model, followed by quantitative comparison using local and integrated squared residuals.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the $\varphi^4$ scalar field model, governed by a non-linear equation of motion, and compares its solutions to those derived from the integrable sine-Gordon model.
key_observables: Local field equation residuals ($R_A$) and integrated squared residuals ($\mathcal{R}_A$), which quantify the deviation from the $\varphi^4$ equation of motion.
important_parameters: Initial half-separation ($d$) and velocity ($v$), analyzed particularly in the small separation limit ($d \lesssim 1.5$).
main_assumptions: The resulting mapped fields are mathematically consistent approximations but are not exact solutions to the $\varphi^4$ equation of motion because the target theory is non-integrable.

paper_structure: The paper establishes the mapping from sG to $\varphi^4$, develops two classes of deformed solutions (Class I and II), and then rigorously compares these analytical approximations against the standard superposition Ansatz using residual analysis to quantify accuracy.
why_interesting: The techniques used—mapping exact solutions from integrable systems to non-integrable ones—are highly relevant for developing physically motivated initial conditions for complex non-linear dynamics simulations in quantum field theory.

Figure 2: Field profiles φ(x, t0) evaluated at the approach-phase time t0(d) = −d/v for three representative half-separations: (a) d = 0.4, (b) d = 1.0, and (c) d = 2.0, with fixed velocity v = 0.2. In each panel, the black solid, blue dashed, and red dot-dashed curves denote φsup in Eq. (15), φ(I) in Eq. (12), and φ(II) in Eq. (14), respectively. The profiles cover the strong-overlap, intermediate, and weak-overlap regimes and are displayed with the same ordering used in the residual analysis.

Figure 3: Local residual profiles RA(x; d, v) as functions of x at v = 0.2 for three representative half-separations: (a) d = 0.4, (b) d = 1.0, and (c) d = 2.0. In each panel, Rsup is represented by the black solid curve, RI by the blue dashed curve, and RII by the red dot-dashed curve. These residuals are defined in Eqs. (21), (22), and (25), respectively. The panels show the overall reduction of the residual amplitudes as the overlap decreases and illustrate the distinct spatial structures generated by the three Ansatzes.

Figure 4: Integrated squared residuals RA(d, v), defined in Eq. (28), as functions of the half-separation d ≤2 for (a) v = 0.1, (b) v = 0.2, and (c) v = 0.5. The black solid, blue dashed, and red dot-dashed curves correspond to the standard superposition (A = sup), Class I (A = I), and Class II (A = II), respectively. The main semi-logarithmic panels illustrate the global behavior and decay of the residuals across all three prescriptions. Insets display Rsup and RI on a linear scale in the strongly nonlinear regime (0.1 ≤d ≤0.9), highlighting that the Class I configuration significantly reduces the residual (by more than a factor of two at low velocities) compared to standard superposition.
